How Spring Security works

Spring Security is a chain of servlet filters that runs before your controller. It does two checks on every request:

  1. Authentication asks "who are you?" and fails with 401.
  2. Authorization asks "are you allowed here?" and fails with 403.

Request flow

  • Tomcat hands the request to DelegatingFilterProxy, which passes it to FilterChainProxy.
  • FilterChainProxy picks the first matching SecurityFilterChain, and its filters run in a fixed order.
  • The authentication filters (form login, Basic, etc.) work out the user and store it in the SecurityContext.
  • AuthorizationFilter runs last and checks the user's roles against your URL rules.
  • If everything passes, DispatcherServlet calls your controller.

How JWT works in Spring Security

A JWT (JSON Web Token) is a signed string that proves who the user is, so the server doesn't need to keep a session. It has three parts joined by dots:

  • Header: the signing algorithm.
  • Payload: claims such as the username, roles and expiry time.
  • Signature: a hash of the first two parts made with a secret key.

The payload is signed, not encrypted. Anyone can read it, but nobody can change it without breaking the signature, so never put secrets in it.

Step A: login, once

  1. The client sends POST /login with the username and password.
  2. AuthenticationManager passes the attempt to the AuthenticationProvider. This is the same provider flow as in the earlier diagram, using UserDetailsService and PasswordEncoder.
  3. If the credentials are valid, your JwtService builds the payload, signs it and returns the token in the response. If they are wrong, the client gets a 401 and no token.

Step B: every later request

  1. The client sends Authorization: Bearer <token>.
  2. Your JwtAuthenticationFilter runs before UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter. It reads the header and checks that the signature matches and the token hasn't expired. A bad or expired token gets a 401.
  3. The filter builds an Authentication from the payload (user and roles) and stores it in the SecurityContext. There is no password check and no database call.
  4. AuthorizationFilter checks the roles against your URL rules, and a missing role gets a 403. Then the controller runs.

Auto-configuration

Spring Boot loads candidate configuration classes and registers beans only when conditions pass.

Key Concepts Summary

  1. Trigger: @EnableAutoConfiguration
    • Usually included automatically via @SpringBootApplication.
    • Triggers two meta-annotations:
      • @AutoConfigurationPackage: Registers the base package scanning location for client beans.
      • @Import(EnableAutoConfigurationImportSelector.class): Drives the dynamic bean selection and loading process.
  2. Configuration Lookup: META-INF/spring.factories
    • The EnableAutoConfigurationImportSelector delegates to SpringFactoriesLoader.loadFactoryNames().
    • It scans classpath dependencies (mainly spring-boot-autoconfigure.jar) inside META-INF/spring.factories under the key org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.EnableAutoConfiguration.
  3. Conditional Registration: @ConditionalOnXxx
    • Found configuration classes are not blindly loaded into the Spring container. They are evaluated against conditional annotations:
      • @ConditionalOnClass: Evaluates true if a specific class exists on the application's runtime classpath (typically brought in by starter dependencies).
      • @ConditionalOnProperty: Evaluates true if a configuration property matches expected values in application.properties or application.yml.
      • @ConditionalOnMissingBean: Evaluates true if the application context does not already define a user-provided bean for that type (allowing custom overrides).
  4. Bean Initialization
    • If all conditions evaluate to true, the auto-configuration class is loaded and its @Bean definition methods register beans automatically into the Spring Application Context.

Annotations

Spring Boot annotations grouped into core bootstrap, ordering control and conditional checks.

Key Spring Boot Annotations

  • Core & Bootstrap Annotations
    • @SpringBootApplication: Enables auto-configuration, component scanning, and extra bean registration in a single main setup class.
    • @EnableAutoConfiguration: Triggers Spring Boot's mechanism to guess and configure beans based on runtime classpath dependencies.
    • @SpringBootConfiguration: Serves as a Spring Boot-specific alternative to standard @Configuration so settings can be automatically located.
    • @ImportAutoConfiguration: Applies only specifically listed auto-configuration classes instead of running full auto-configuration.
  • Auto-Configuration Ordering Annotations
    • @AutoConfigureBefore / @AutoConfigureAfter: Specifies the execution order of auto-configuration classes relative to one another.
    • @AutoConfigureOrder: Assigns a numerical priority order to auto-configuration classes.
  • Conditional Annotations (@ConditionalOn...)
    • @ConditionalOnClass / @ConditionalOnMissingClass: Registers beans/configurations based on whether specified classes are present or missing from the classpath.
    • @ConditionalOnBean / @ConditionalOnMissingBean: Registers beans based on whether target beans are already defined in the application context.
    • @ConditionalOnProperty: Includes configuration based on specific property names and values defined in application properties.
    • @ConditionalOnWebApplication / @ConditionalOnNotWebApplication: Triggers configuration depending on whether the app is a web-based application.
    • @ConditionalOnResource: Loads configuration only when specified static files or resources exist on the classpath.
    • @ConditionalOnExpression: Evaluates a SpEL (Spring Expression Language) condition to decide bean registration.
    • @ConditionalOnCloudPlatform: Applies configuration only when running on an active target cloud platform (e.g., Cloud Foundry).

Spring Doesn’t Recommend @Autowired Anymore

Field injection hides dependencies, allows mutability and is hard to test. Constructor injection is recommended.

Pattern language

Microservice patterns grouped by decomposition, data, communication, discovery, observability and deployment.

Key Microservice Patterns

  • Decomposition Patterns
    • Decompose by Business Capability: Structures services around business functions (e.g., Order Management, Shipping).
    • Decompose by Subdomain: Groups services around DDD bounded contexts.
  • Data Management Patterns
    • Database per Service: Keeps each service's data private for loose coupling.
    • Shared Database: One database for many services; an anti-pattern, but used during migration.
    • Saga Pattern: Keeps data consistent across services using local transactions triggered by events.
    • API Composition: An aggregator queries multiple services and joins results in memory.
    • CQRS (Command Query Responsibility Segregation): Separates read and write operations into distinct data models.
    • Event Sourcing: Stores state as a sequence of state-changing events.
  • Communication & API Patterns
    • Remote Procedure Invocation (RPI): Synchronous calls using REST or gRPC.
    • Messaging: Asynchronous communication through message channels and brokers.
    • API Gateway: Single entry point that routes, translates and secures client requests.
    • Backend for Frontend (BFF): Gateways tailored to specific clients (e.g., mobile vs. web).
  • Service Discovery & Registration
    • Client-Side Discovery: Clients query the service registry directly.
    • Server-Side Discovery: Clients call a router/load balancer that queries the registry and proxies traffic.
    • Self Registration: Instances register and deregister themselves.
    • 3rd Party Registration: An external registrar registers and deregisters instances.
  • Observability & Reliability Patterns
    • Circuit Breaker: Returns errors immediately when a downstream service is unresponsive, preventing cascading failures.
    • Distributed Tracing: Assigns unique IDs to requests to trace calls across services.
    • Log Aggregation: Centralizes logs from all instances into a searchable store.
    • Health Check API: Endpoint that reports service status for orchestration checks.
  • Refactoring & Deployment Patterns
    • Strangler Fig Pattern: Gradually replaces monolith functions with microservices until the monolith is retired.
    • Transactional Outbox: Writes events to an outbox table in a local transaction, then publishes to a broker.
    • Microservice Chassis: Reusable framework for cross-cutting concerns (logging, metrics, discovery).

Scaling and databases

Scale out with stateless servers, and scale the database one step at a time.

Vertical vs Horizontal Scaling

  • Vertical Scaling (Scale Up): Increases the hardware power (CPU, RAM, storage) of a single server, making it simple to set up but limited by physical hardware limits and vulnerable to a single point of failure.
  • Horizontal Scaling (Scale Out): Adds more servers to distribute user traffic across multiple machines via a load balancer, providing near-unlimited growth and fault tolerance at the cost of higher system complexity.

Why Scaling Out Needs Stateless Servers?

  • The goal of scaling out (horizontal scaling): Add more servers so the load balancer can spread requests across any of them, freely and interchangeably.
  • The problem: state breaks this
    • State = data remembered between requests (e.g., a user's cart, login session).
    • If a server stores this in its own memory, it is stateful.
    • Example: user adds a phone to cart, the request goes to Server A, and the cart is saved only on A. The next request goes to Server B, which knows nothing about the cart, so the user sees an empty cart.
  • Why this breaks scaling
    • The load balancer can no longer send a request to any server. It would need to always route the same user to the same server.
    • That defeats the purpose of horizontal scaling, which relies on interchangeable servers.
  • The fix: make servers stateless
    • Move all state out of individual servers into a shared store (like Redis or a database).
    • Every server reads and writes the same shared data instead of keeping its own copy.

Database Scaling Strategy

  • 🌐 CDN: Global edge servers deliver static assets (images, scripts) close to users, stripping heavy traffic off your core system.
  • ⚡ Cache (e.g., Redis): RAM-based storage that absorbs up to 80% of DB reads for frequent data.
  • 📖 Read Replicas: DB clones handle read traffic while a single Primary DB handles writes.
  • 🧩 Sharding: Splits data across separate DBs (e.g., Shard 1: IDs 1–1M) when writes or storage outgrow one machine.
  • 📬 Message Queues: Buffers slow work (emails, image processing) for background workers so users get instant responses.
  • 🔄 Autoscaling: Dynamically spins stateless app servers up or down based on CPU metrics (e.g., 20 servers at lunch, 5 at night).
  • ⚠️ Rule of Thumb: Max out CDNs, Caching, Queues, and Replicas first. Sharding handles extreme scale but adds severe query and rebalancing complexity.

API Gateway

An API Gateway is the single entry point between clients and your microservices. Clients talk to one address, and the gateway handles routing and the shared checks so each service doesn't have to.

Why it exists

Without a gateway, every client must know the address of every service, and each service repeats the same work: login checks, rate limits, logging. A web page that needs data from three services makes three calls. With a gateway, the client makes one call and the gateway does the rest. It acts like a reverse proxy with extra features.

How it works

  1. The client sends a request to the gateway, for example GET /api/orders/42.
  2. Authenticate: the gateway validates the token (for example a JWT). A bad token gets a 401 and the request stops here.
  3. Protect: it applies rate limits so one client cannot flood the system. Too many requests get a 429.
  4. Route: it matches the URL path to a service, asks the service registry for healthy instances and picks one (load balancing).
  5. Forward: it calls the service. For some requests it calls several services and merges the results into one response.
  6. Respond: it can transform or cache the response, records logs and metrics, and returns the result to the client.

Functionality

RoutingMaps URLs and headers to the right service, so clients never see internal addresses.
Authentication and authorizationChecks tokens once at the edge, so services receive only trusted requests.
Rate limitingCaps requests per client or per key to protect services from overload and abuse.
Load balancing and discoverySpreads traffic across service instances found through the service registry.
AggregationCombines results from several services into a single response, which means fewer round trips.
Request and response transformationChanges formats or protocols, for example REST for clients and gRPC inside.
CachingStores common responses so repeated requests never reach the service.
SSL/TLS terminationHandles HTTPS at the edge so internal traffic stays simple.
ResilienceTimeouts, retries and circuit breakers stop one slow service from taking everything down.
ObservabilityCentral place for access logs, metrics and trace IDs on every request.

Example: Spring Cloud Gateway route

spring:
  cloud:
    gateway:
      routes:
        - id: order-service
          uri: lb://order-service        # looked up in the service registry
          predicates:
            - Path=/api/orders/**        # match this URL
          filters:
            - StripPrefix=1              # remove /api before forwarding

Trade-offs

  • Single point of failure: run several gateway instances behind a load balancer.
  • Extra network hop: adds a little latency to every request.
  • Keep it thin: put only cross-cutting concerns in the gateway. Business logic belongs in the services, or the gateway becomes a new monolith.
  • Backend for Frontend (BFF): a variation with one gateway per client type, such as one for mobile and one for web.

Common choices: Spring Cloud Gateway, Kong, NGINX and AWS API Gateway.
